summary: Top Traders Unplugged ep. 423 (Oct 2026): French yield spike and sovereign debt, why bond selloff is a return to normal (real rate + inflation + term premium), convenience yield erosion, geo-economic fragmentation raising diversification for trend following, commodity stock-outs, and AI/ML alpha crowding versus trend following.

coverage.note: FIMO vs FOMO, discount rate; JGB demand
Trend following and bond regime; institutional structure
Hedgers vs speculators; performance numbers; Nobel intro
Intermediation capital, dealer warehousing; Mehrling tribute
Benign 90s vs crises of 80s-90s (omitted from crisis-alpha stories)
Upheavals and supercycles; bond selloff return to normal
Nominal yield build-up; term premium; credit to GDP
Fiscal debt; hedge fund role in bonds; convenience yield
Convenience yield, dollar, gold, geoeconomics intro

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we are seeing kind of record yields in in France. I mean, I think we're trading now the 10 years just about 5% now in France.
claims.claim: French 10-year yields near 5%, a 24-year high, amid unrest show sovereign debt of a large country being tested, reminiscent of past euro-area crises, and change how investors view safe assets.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: Your cost of capital it can't be lower than than treasuries.
claims.claim: Stocks rise despite higher discount rates only because earnings growth (FIMO) exceeds the discount-rate effect; if earnings momentum stops, the discount rate becomes dominant and valuations fall.
claims.direction: equities down if earnings momentum stalls

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we saw a record demand for 20-year JGBs at the latest auction.
claims.claim: Strong Japanese 20-year JGB auction demand (about six times covered) pulled yields down and hurt trend followers' fixed-income positions in early Q4.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: trend followers only make, uh, money when bond prices are rallying
claims.claim: The belief that trend following only profits when bonds rally (Niederhoffer) reflected the 1981-2020 secular decline in yields; with a return to normal, bond markets are two-way and shorts can pay.
claims.conditions: regime of secular rates trend vs normal
claims.testable: yes - test trend returns across rate regimes

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: you just have to be patient as as Katie and I talked about last week I think it was with the latest paper from Quantica where they talk about you know the importance of time in trend following
claims.claim: Markets that long frustrate trend followers (cocoa shorts) later give big trends, so time in the market matters more than timing trend following.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the composition of markets, of who is trading in a market, will have a big impact on whether you can make money on trend following
claims.claim: Trend profitability depends on market institutional structure: who trades (hedgers vs speculators, governments vs profit maximizers) shapes trend persistence.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: markets that have more hedgers relative to speculators, a trend follower could do better because you're you're taking the other side of uh of of hedgers
claims.claim: Markets with more hedgers relative to speculators favor trend followers, who take the other side of hedgers' positions.
claims.direction: long trend followers where hedgers dominate

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my trend barometer finished at 40, so at the lower end of neutral.
claims.claim: A trend barometer at 40 is lower-neutral; CTA index about -1% in October but about +14% YTD.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: they received it for basically providing what we'll call the micro foundations for macroeconomics.
claims.claim: Hall and Woodford won the Nobel for micro foundations of macro; trend followers should analogously study the micro foundations of markets: who trades, exchange rules and how policy changes profit-maximizing behavior.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: Woodford, his importance was on interest rate controls, and he was the one who probably
claims.claim: Woodford's natural rate of interest framework underlies central bank policy: raise or cut rates relative to the natural rate to affect aggregate demand and use forward guidance.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: capital flows matter. And we should as as some people would say in crime drama say you need to follow the money.
claims.claim: Following Mehrling's money view, the plumbing of money (payment systems, dealer financing, shadow banking) and capital flows drive markets.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: our you know responsibility is to identify the type of environment we're in. To say are we more susceptible to a crisis?
claims.claim: Rather than measuring crisis alpha after the fact, identify the environment: shortage of dealer/bank intermediation capital raises susceptibility to a crisis.
claims.indicator: intermediation capital of banks and primary dealers

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: If you can't serve your warehouse function, then that means is that you're going to have to move from seller to buyer
claims.claim: When capital-constrained dealers cannot warehouse risk, sellers cannot find buyers except in a disorderly way, causing dislocations in bonds and commodities, which can create trends.
claims.indicator: dealer balance sheet constraint, repo stress

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: you need a global hegemon who can be and be able to pre a place structure in our global financial markets.
claims.claim: Post-WWII globalization relied on a dominant dollar and institutions (World Bank, IMF) that mitigated dislocations; trend followers should be agnostic about globalization and just exploit the environment.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the kind of the peak 3-5 years of of everything being perfect and quiet and calm uh was was pretty challenging.
claims.claim: Peak globalization with stable inflation and falling rates produced a quiet period for trend followers, with no big drawdowns but weak returns.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's funny because we never really talk about them in the our industry.
claims.claim: Crisis alpha studies in the trend industry start with the tech bubble and ignore 1980s-90s upheavals (Plaza Accord, S&L, 1987 crash, ERM, Tequila, Asia 1998), which were also volatile and relevant to trend following.
claims.conditions: sample starting in 2000 omits earlier crises

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: concentrated dislocation in markets, but there's also upheavals that occur because there's changes in the behavior of markets that it lead to very long-term trends.
claims.claim: Distinguish crises (concentrated dislocations) from upheavals such as commodity supercycles caused by underinvestment in capital expenditure, which produce long grinding trends that suit trend following.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the current environment is a return to normalcy.
claims.claim: The bond sell-off is a return to normal rates after two decades of near-zero and negative yields, which were the oddity.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: what should a nominal rate be? It should be equal to the real rate plus expected inflation plus some type of term premium or risk premium.
claims.claim: Fair nominal yield equals real rate (~2-2.5%) plus expected inflation (~3%) plus a term premium, implying about 5-5.5% on long Treasuries, close to current levels.
claims.indicator: nominal yield = real rate + expected inflation + term premium

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: When the stock bond correlation is more positive, there should be more of a term premium or a risk premium.
claims.claim: A positive stock-bond covariance and higher bond volatility should raise the term premium, unlike the negative-correlation era of near-zero term premia.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: private markets are maybe crowding out some of the public markets.
claims.claim: Strong demand for debt in private markets crowds out public markets, while private sector credit-to-GDP is controlled but public debt-to-GDP keeps rising (BIS early-warning indicator).

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: we're not getting that and then on top of that you add in the cost of debt.
claims.claim: Governments are not running primary surpluses after recessions and interest costs are crowding out other spending (also in France and Japan), pressuring long-term yields.
claims.indicator: primary balance, interest share of budget

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: are much more active in the debt markets through basis trading and financing.
claims.claim: Hedge funds (multi-strat pods) are now more active in bonds via basis trades and are more sensitive to losses than central banks, so demand is more elastic and bond moves could be large either way.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: when there's a crisis, the convenience yield goes up because there's a tremendous amount of movement
claims.claim: The convenience yield on safe assets rises in crisis from increased demand, but shrinks as the government issues more safe debt.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: that what was perceived as a convenience yield has may have disappeared.
claims.claim: The convenience yield has disappeared at the long end of the Treasury curve and survives mainly in bills, explaining heavier bill issuance.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the dollar regime is is breaking and there's more of we'll call it multi-polarity
claims.claim: Central bank reserve managers are reducing dollar exposure toward multi-polarity, diminishing the dollar's convenience yield relatively.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: is France a safe asset in by any stretch of the imagination?
claims.claim: France is no longer clearly a European safe asset and southern European bonds may be less risky than assumed.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: we would expect that people would be pouring more money into gold right now, and yet it it's off its highs from the summer.
claims.claim: Gold, expected to benefit from geopolitical trouble, fell back from above $5000 to about $4100, challenging its safe haven reputation in the last 6 months.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: if the world becomes more fragmented and dislocated, we should sort of see that diversification increases in markets. Markets are going to become more decoupled.
claims.claim: Geo-economic fragmentation (tariffs, sanctions, capital controls) reduces cross-market correlation, raising diversification for trend following; less fragmentation raises correlation, so correlation matrices must reflect geoeconomics.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: when markets are more divergent as we see at the moment, so to speak, um as you rightly say, um the the correlation between generally speaking um positions and holdings in these um strategies uh tend to come down
claims.claim: Low correlation between trend positions allows more risk-taking and strong performance; when highly correlated, reduce risk because reversal risk rises.
claims.direction: scale risk up when correlations low, down when high

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: if we become more fragmented, if there's a breakdown in in we'll say global hegemony,
claims.claim: Fragmentation creates value in trading the same commodity at different locations (London vs New York copper, cocoa) because delivery points and tariffs cause divergence.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the real problem in commodities is not what is produced, but it's what the inventories look like
claims.claim: Commodity price spikes are driven by stock-out fears: low inventories (e.g. Europe winter gas below five-year norms) lead to hoarding and parabolic moves.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: crisis alpha with a with a big C and then you can say crisis alpha with a small C which would be on a on a market-by-market basis.
claims.claim: Market-specific 'crisis alpha' arises in markets with few substitutes (diesel, cocoa) and low inventories, so look at substitutability to find nonlinear spikes.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: of hedge fund managers, how many people are using machine learning to to find alpha
claims.claim: Machine learning use is above 90% among hedge funds; alpha half-life shortens as everyone adopts the same models.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: we may not have the same thing as a as an alpha half-life
claims.claim: Trend following has no alpha half-life since it waits for dislocations; low returns while waiting are the cost of doing business.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: Which is called the Red Queen problem
claims.claim: Crowded ML strategies force a rising compute budget to find new models, the Red Queen problem.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: they looked at the 13F filings from a lot of major hedge funds and they noticed is that there's an increasing similarity in the positions
claims.claim: 13F filings show increasing similarity in hedge fund equity positions, evidence that ML strategies are crowding.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: I have to have a strategy that can be enduring beyond this crowding of alpha
claims.claim: Trend following is distinct from ML alpha seeking; use ML to capture trends but ensure the strategy outlasts alpha crowding.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: I'll ask something from from AI and then I'll use chat GPT, I'll use Gemini, I'll use you know Grok and then I'll use Claude
claims.claim: Asking multiple AI models the same question gives similar answers, so AI-derived signals risk common-model herding; fine for facts but unreliable for novel ideas.
